issues.legal_issue: Reliable eyewitness testimony supported by medical evidence establishes the shooting despite embellishment in the account of how the dispute began and despite witnesses who arrived after the shooting.
material_facts: Two witnesses who were present in the field testified that the shooter fired at the deceased and that two shots struck him.
The deceased’s injuries and the medical evidence were consistent with those witnesses’ account of the shooting.
The account that the shooter deliberately let an animal graze the crop may have been exaggerated; the dispute could have begun when the animal strayed into the field.
Other witnesses who claimed to have seen the occurrence arrived after it was over.
issues.conclusion: The embellished account of the dispute’s beginning did not undermine proof of the shooting, and the conviction for causing the deceased’s death was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: An exaggerated account of the genesis of an incident does not require rejection of the prosecution case when reliable witnesses prove the offence itself and their evidence is consistent with medical evidence. No earlier case was relied on for this principle.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal concerns a conviction, reliable eyewitness identification supported by medical evidence can sustain the conviction despite embellishment in the account of how the dispute began.

issues.legal_issue: Mere presence in an armed group does not establish shared responsibility for murder where the evidence does not prove that murder was the group’s common object or that its members knew murder was likely.
material_facts: After an argument, the lead assailant returned within minutes with armed companions and immediately shot the deceased.
The other armed companions did not fire at the deceased or at the people standing near him, and no other act by them showed an intention to kill or injure those people.
The companions later fired indiscriminately, causing simple injuries to villagers, but the evidence did not show that they shared a plan to kill the deceased.
The court found that the circumstances did not establish that the armed companions had formed an unlawful assembly with the common object of murder.
issues.conclusion: The convictions for murder on the basis of shared liability were set aside because the evidence did not establish the required common object or knowledge; the convictions for unlawful assembly were also set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, constructive liability requires proof that an offence was committed by a member of an unlawful assembly and that it was committed in prosecution of the assembly’s common object or was an offence the members knew was likely to be committed. Mere membership or presence with weapons is insufficient. The court relied on no earlier case for this principle.

predicates.companions_do_not_attack_the_deceased_or: The evidence does not show the companions attacking the deceased or the people standing near the deceased.
predicates.evidence_does_not_establish_shared_murde: The evidence does not establish that the group shared an object to commit murder or knew that murder was likely.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal, armed companions are not liable for murder through shared group responsibility when the evidence does not establish a shared murder object or knowledge that murder was likely.

issues.legal_issue: Indiscriminate firing that causes simple injuries does not constitute attempted murder without evidence of an intention or knowledge to cause death and an act done toward that end.
material_facts: The evidence showed that two accused fired indiscriminately in an open area and that villagers suffered simple firearm injuries.
The injured witnesses did not identify either accused as the person who caused their injuries, and the injured people had not seen the firing.
There was no evidence about the distance from which the firing took place or that the accused aimed at any particular injured person.
The evidence established the injuries but did not establish an intention or knowledge to commit murder.
issues.conclusion: The convictions for attempted murder were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 307 of the Indian Penal Code requires an intention or knowledge of the kind necessary to constitute murder and an act done toward committing murder. Intention may be inferred from relevant circumstances, including the weapon, the location and nature of the injuries, and the circumstances of the incident; the consequence of the act alone does not establish the required intention or knowledge. No earlier case was relied on for this principle.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal, firing that causes only simple injuries does not establish attempted-murder liability when the injured people do not identify the shooters and the evidence does not show an intention or knowledge to cause death.

issues.legal_issue: Common intention to cause injury can develop at the scene during an incident, making participants liable for injuries caused by their acts in furtherance of that shared intention.
material_facts: After the lead assailant shot and seriously injured the deceased, the other accused began firing indiscriminately and another participant threw a spear.
The court found that the participants acted to ward off an anticipated attack by the complainant party and nearby villagers, and that their shared intention developed at the scene after the shooting.
The indiscriminate firing caused simple injuries to villagers, although the evidence did not link a particular injury to a particular firearm user.
issues.conclusion: The participants were convicted of causing hurt in furtherance of their common intention.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 324 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, persons may be liable for hurt caused by acts done in furtherance of their common intention. The common intention may develop at the scene during the occurrence. The court reasoned that those using firearms indiscriminately in an open area could be presumed to know that bodily injury was likely, and individual attribution of each injury was not required where the injuries resulted from acts in furtherance of the shared intention. No earlier case was relied on for this principle.

issues.definition: When participants form a shared intention during an incident and their joint use of weapons to ward off anticipated retaliation causes bodily injuries, they are guilty of causing hurt in furtherance of that shared intention.

issues.legal_issue: An irregular examination of an accused about incriminating evidence does not entitle the accused to relief when no prejudice from the irregularity is established.
material_facts: The trial court recorded the accused persons’ statements in a cursory and unsatisfactory manner, without adequately putting the incriminating circumstances to them for explanation.
No argument based on the defective statements had been advanced in the trial court or the High Court.
No prejudice caused by the defective statements was identified on appeal.
issues.conclusion: The accused were not entitled to relief on account of the irregular statements.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the court must give an accused a personal opportunity to explain circumstances appearing in the evidence. Incriminating evidence cannot be relied on for conviction if that opportunity is not afforded. However, the court granted no benefit in this case because the accused did not establish prejudice from the irregularity. No earlier case was relied on for this principle.
